summary: This informational document defines requirements for standards on Energy Management, covering monitoring and control functions. Monitoring includes identifying energy-managed devices and components and their power states, inlets, outlets, power, and energy. Control includes functions such as controlling power states.

plainLanguage.summary: Network equipment uses power, and operators need a consistent way to measure and manage it. This RFC lists what future energy-management standards should be able to report and control.

subtitle: Requirements for standards that monitor and control energy use in networked equipment.

tldr.problem: Energy management standards need consistent ways to identify devices, report their energy-related information, and control their power states and supplies.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets requirements for monitoring devices and components, describing power and energy measurements, and controlling the same or other entities.
tldr.outcome: It specifies requirements for standards, not features that every implementation must provide.

facts.label: Monitoring subjects
facts.value: Devices, components, power interfaces, and batteries

sections.title: Requirements for Energy Management Standards
sections.content:
RFC 6988 defines requirements for standards that support energy management of network devices and their components. It covers monitoring, such as identifying equipment and reporting its power state or energy use, and control, such as changing a power state.

The document addresses standards specifications, not implementation conformance. Later standards define which features are mandatory, recommended, or optional for a product.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC lists what energy-management standards should support. It does not require every device to implement every feature.

sections.title: Identifying Devices and Components
sections.content:
A management system needs to identify both whole devices and their components. Examples include a router, a line card, a battery, or a device connected through a gateway. The standard must support identifiers that remain unique when information is collected.

Energy information can be reported for a complete device or for an individual part. A device that reports information about another device must identify that other device as well.
sections.plainLanguage: A management system needs to know which device or component each measurement describes. Standards should support reporting about both whole devices and individual parts.

sections.title: Monitoring Power, Energy, and State
sections.content:
The requirements cover information about devices, power inlets and outlets, power measurements, energy, power states, batteries, and time series. A report should distinguish a measured value from an estimate and provide information about its accuracy. Energy values also need a time interval.

A power interface may receive power, provide it, or do both. Standards should identify the connections between power inlets and outlets. Battery information can include charge and charging state, and power-state information can include the states supported by an entity.
sections.plainLanguage: Monitoring includes how much power a device uses, how much energy it used over time, and which power state it is in. The report should explain whether a value was measured or estimated.

sections.title: Controlling Devices and Their Power
sections.content:
Energy management standards must support requests to change an entity's power state. They must also support switching power supplies at interfaces that provide power to other devices. A power distribution unit or a Power over Ethernet switch may control a device through its outlet or port.

Not all measurements or controls are available from the entity being managed. A meter or upstream device may report on or control other entities. Abruptly switching off a power supply can have serious consequences, so these actions require careful protection.
sections.plainLanguage: A management system may ask a device to change its power state or ask another device to switch its power supply. Turning off power can affect connected equipment, so these commands need protection.

sections.title: Protecting Energy Data and Controls
sections.content:
Changing a power state or supply can disrupt connected equipment. Standards must provide authentication, authorization, and integrity protection for control actions. Monitoring data also needs access controls and protection while it is transmitted or stored.

Some entities are not secure enough to connect directly to the public Internet. The standard must support isolating them behind a secure gateway or disabling sensitive functions in environments that do not provide adequate protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Only authorized users should be able to change a device's power state. Monitoring information also needs protection, and insecure devices may need to sit behind a secure gateway.
